A Layer of Neurons Is a Matrix

A neuron is a rule that converts a point into a score. Neurons become the rows of a matrix, and applying them to the data becomes one product.

This meeting, in one sentence

A layer of neurons is a matrix, and applying it to data is one product: written in NumPy, written again in PyTorch, run on a GPU, and counted.

  • Meeting 10 stored data as a matrix X with one point in each row. Today a neuron, a rule that converts a point into a score, is stored as a row of a matrix W.
  • Three acts: the layer in NumPy, on the pixels of your group's image; the same layer in PyTorch and on a GPU; what the product costs.
  • For each act: slides, then a Colab block in the class notebook, then a post. Ask Colab for a GPU before you run anything: the class notebook says how.
Notes. Two minutes. The GPU is asked for first because Colab erases a session when its runtime type changes.
CS 301 · Meeting 11 · Act 1 · A Layer of Neurons Is a Matrix2 / 19

One neuron, one point

A neuron has one weight for each coordinate of a point, and one more number, its bias. On a point x with m coordinates it computes the score

s=w1x1+w2x2+…+wmxm+b
  • The neuron fires when s ≥ 0. Every coordinate is multiplied by its weight; the products and the bias are added.
  • Today a point is one pixel of the group's image, with m = 3 coordinates: red, green, blue. The grey rule of meeting 10 is the neuron with the weights 0.299, 0.587, 0.114 and the bias 0.
the pixel   x = [0.56 0.39 0.1 ]  (red, green, blue)
the weights w = [0.299 0.587 0.114]  and the bias b = 0.0
Notes. The hand computation of the act: ask for the score of this pixel. Three products, their sum, the bias.
CS 301 · Meeting 11 · Act 1 · A Layer of Neurons Is a Matrix3 / 19

The same score, with matrices

s=wTx+b
  • In linear algebra x and w are columns, m × 1. The transpose wT holds the same numbers as a row, 1 × m. A row times a column is one number: the sum of the products of matching entries.
  • The shapes say why the transpose is there: (1 × m)(m × 1) is 1 × 1. Without it, (m × 1)(m × 1) is not defined.
  • In NumPy, w_grey and x have one dimension, shape (3,): neither a row nor a column. @ between them is their dot product, and such an array is its own transpose.
s_one = w_grey @ x + b_grey          # the dot product of the weights and the point, plus the bias
print(f"s = {s_one:.3f}")
print("shape of w_grey:", w_grey.shape, "  shape of x:", x.shape)

s = 0.411
shape of w_grey: (3,)   shape of x: (3,)

One neuron, many points

X = image.reshape(-1, 3)                 # one row for each pixel
n, m = X.shape
print(f"shape of X: {X.shape}, which is n = {n:,} points with m = {m} coordinates")

s_grey = X @ w_grey + b_grey             # the scores of the grey neuron on all the points
print("shape of X @ w_grey + b_grey:", s_grey.shape)

shape of X: (320640, 3), which is n = 320,640 points with m = 3 coordinates
shape of X @ w_grey + b_grey: (320640,)
the scores of the first five points: [0.482 0.532 0.5   0.482 0.477]
  • image.reshape(-1, 3) writes the pixels as the rows of X: n points with m = 3 coordinates, n = height × width.
  • X @ w_grey is one score for each point, n numbers. + b_grey adds one number to all of them: broadcasting, as v + 10 in meeting 10.
CS 301 · Meeting 11 · Act 1 · A Layer of Neurons Is a Matrix5 / 19

The same scores, with matrices

s=Xw+b1
  • X is n × m and w is m × 1, so Xw is n × 1. Entry i is row i of X times w. Row i of X is the point xi written as a row, xiT, and xiTw is the same number as wTxi. The transpose has moved from the weights to the point, because the data stores each point as a row.
  • 1 is a column of n ones: the mathematics needs it in order to add the single number b to each of the n scores. NumPy's broadcasting does the same.
Notes. The picture of the scores is the grey image of meeting 10: the largest difference is below 0.005.

A neuron that fires

b_bright = -s_grey.mean()                        # minus the mean brightness of the image
fires = X @ w_grey + b_bright >= 0               # True for the points on which the neuron fires
print(f"bias {b_bright:.3f}: the neuron fires on {fires.mean():.1%} of the {n:,} pixels")

bias -0.518: the neuron fires on 53.1% of the 320,640 pixels

A brightness is never negative, so with the bias 0 the grey neuron fires on every pixel. With the bias −(mean brightness) it fires on the pixels brighter than the average. θ = −b is the threshold of the neuron.

CS 301 · Meeting 11 · Act 1 · A Layer of Neurons Is a Matrix7 / 19

Two ways to store the points

by_rows = X @ w_grey + b_bright          # points as rows: X has shape (n, m)
by_columns = w_grey @ X.T + b_bright     # points as columns: X.T has shape (m, n)

shape of X: (320640, 3)   shape of X.T: (3, 320640)
The two results are equal: True
w_grey @ X fails: w_grey has 3 entries and X has 320,640 rows, so the shapes do not fit
  • In this course, as in pandas, NumPy and PyTorch, a point is a row of X, and the scores are Xw + b.
  • Many books store a point as a column. Their data matrix is XT, m × n, and the same scores are written wTX + b.
  • w_grey @ X fails: 3 entries against n rows. The shapes do not fit.
Notes. Say the convention once and keep it on the board for the whole meeting: X is (n, m), W is (K, m).
CS 301 · Meeting 11 · Act 1 · A Layer of Neurons Is a Matrix8 / 19

Many neurons, one point

A layer is a set of K neurons that read the same point. Row j of W holds the weights of neuron j, as a row of X holds a point, and b holds the K biases. The K scores of a point are s = Wx + b: W is K × m and x is m × 1, so Wx is K × 1, and so is b. Nothing is repeated.

K = 5
C = reference_colours(X, K)              # K rows and 3 columns: the reference colours, darkest first
W = C.copy()                             # the weights of the layer: row j is reference colour j
b = -0.5 * (C ** 2).sum(axis=1)          # the biases of the layer: one number for each neuron

shape of W: (5, 3)   shape of b: (5,)
W =
[[0.32 0.36 0.31]
 [0.63 0.46 0.1 ]
 [0.53 0.53 0.45]
 [0.48 0.57 0.66]
 [0.67 0.65 0.55]]
b = [-0.16 -0.31 -0.38 -0.49 -0.59]

Five reference colours of the image, found by a method called k-means. Neuron j has the weights cj and the bias −½|cj|²: the largest score belongs to the neuron whose colour is nearest to the pixel.

Notes. W is K × m and x is m × 1, so Wx is K × 1, and so is b: the formula works as written, nothing is repeated. Why the nearest colour wins: |x − c|² = x·x − 2(c·x − ½ c·c), and x·x is the same for every neuron. Review Quiz 11 asks the students for this argument; do not give it unless a group asks.

CS 301 · Meeting 11 · Act 1 · A Layer of Neurons Is a Matrix10 / 19

Many neurons, many points

def layer_loops(X, W, b):
    """The scores of the K neurons of a layer on the n points of X, one multiplication at a time."""
    n, m = X.shape
    K = W.shape[0]
    S = np.empty((n, K))
    for i in range(n):                   # every point
        for j in range(K):               # every neuron
            total = b[j]
            for c in range(m):           # every coordinate
                total += W[j, c] * X[i, c]
            S[i, j] = total
    return S
S=XWT+1bT
  • S has n rows and K columns: row i belongs to point i, column j to neuron j. The loops compute it from the definition.
  • X is n × m and WT is m × K, so XWT is n × K. W is transposed because a neuron is a row of W, and the product needs each neuron's weights as a column. 1bT is the biases written again on every row: broadcasting. In Colab you write the three loops as one line.
Notes. Do not write the line. The block has the groups write it, and the check tells them which array to transpose.

When each neuron stands for one possible answer, the answer for a point is the neuron with the largest score: the argmax of its row. C[winner] takes, for every point, the colour of that neuron.

CS 301 · Meeting 11 · Act 1 · A Layer of Neurons Is a Matrix13 / 19

The sigmoid, a function of every entry

σ(s)=11+e−s
def sigmoid(s):
    """The sigmoid of every entry of the array s."""
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-s))
  • σ(0) = 0.5; large positive scores give nearly 1, large negative scores nearly 0. 1 / (1 + np.exp(-s)) acts on every entry: pointwise, and the result keeps the shape of its input.
  • Divided by a temperature T first, the scores spread out: a small T brings the sigmoid close to fires-or-not.
CS 301 · Meeting 11 · Act 1 · A Layer of Neurons Is a Matrix14 / 19

The softmax, a function of every row

pk=eskes1+es2+…+esK
def softmax_rows(S):
    shifted = S - S.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)       # the largest entry of every row becomes 0
    E = np.exp(shifted)
    return E / E.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
  • The K scores of a point become K positive numbers that add to 1, read as probabilities. Every entry of the result depends on all the entries of its row: the softmax is a function of a row, the sigmoid of an entry.
  • Written by an AI assistant to stated requirements: no loop, no library's softmax, and the largest entry of each row subtracted first. Adding one number to all the scores of a point leaves its probabilities as they were; after the subtraction no exponential exceeds 1.
  • axis=1: along each row. keepdims=True: the largest entry and the sum stay a column, shape (n, 1), and broadcast against the n rows.
Notes. The full notebook has each group ask an assistant for this function after class; its check rejects the usual mistakes.
CS 301 · Meeting 11 · Act 1 · A Layer of Neurons Is a Matrix15 / 19

Repaint the image: a small network

Prob = softmax_rows(layer(X, W, b) / T)    # n rows and K columns
new = Prob @ PAINT                         # n rows and 3 columns
  • Each neuron gets a paint, a colour of the group's choice: the rows of PAINT, K × 3. Prob @ PAINT is n × 3: the new colour of a pixel is a mixture of the K paints, each counted with the probability of its neuron.
  • The second product is of the same kind as the first: n points, now with K coordinates, and three neurons. Two layers with a function between them are a small neural network, applied to all the pixels at once.
Notes. At temperature 1 the picture is nearly one flat colour; at 0.002 every pixel takes the paint of its nearest colour.

The four cases

one point x, shape (m,)n points X, shape (n, m)
one neuron: w of shape (m,), b a numberw @ x + b is a numberX @ w + b has shape (n,); b is broadcast
K neurons: W of shape (K, m), b of shape (K,)W @ x + b has shape (K,)X @ W.T + b has shape (n, K); b is broadcast
  • The bias needs help exactly when there are many points: the mathematics writes a column of ones, and NumPy broadcasts.
